result: BsV-NG1 was successfully isolated from a freshwater pond in British Columbia and shown to infect Bodo saltans strain NG with strain specificity. Infection kinetics showed free virus particles appearing 18 hours post-infection, with viral concentrations peaking at 2.5×10^7 particles/ml while host cell density dropped to 25% of controls. The closely related B. saltans strain HFCC12 could not be infected.
evaluation: Claims C37-C43 provide consistent experimental evidence for successful virus isolation and characterization of infection dynamics. The infection kinetics data (C39-C41) are supported by flow cytometry measurements shown in Figure 1, and the strain specificity observation (C42-C43) is based on direct experimental testing with a control strain.

result: TEM analysis revealed BsV is an icosahedral particle approximately 300 nm in diameter with at least six layers including a DNA-containing core, core wall, inner membrane, and double-capsid layer. A ~25 nm halo surrounds the virion, and a possible stargate-like structure is associated with a depression of the virus core, presumably involved in genome release during infection.
evaluation: Claims C44-C49 describe structural features directly observed by TEM (Figure 2A and supplements). The multi-layered structure is well-documented in the images, though the function of the stargate structure (C49) is inferred by comparison to ApMV rather than directly demonstrated for BsV.

result: BsV infection shows spatially organized replication with virus factories consistently located in the cell posterior. During infection progression (6-24 hours), the Golgi apparatus disappeared and the nucleus degraded while the kinetoplast remained intact. Virus factories first appeared at 6h post-infection, expanded to maximum size by 12h when capsid structures appeared, with mature particles observed at 18h coinciding with flow cytometry detection.
evaluation: Claims C50-C59 describe a detailed time course of infection supported by TEM observations at multiple time points (Figure 2B-D and supplements). The temporal progression is internally consistent and correlates with flow cytometry data (Figure 1). The preservation of the kinetoplast (C54) is particularly well-documented in the images.

result: BsV virion assembly involves recruitment of membrane vesicles through the virus factory where capsid proteins accumulate and disrupt vesicles. Vesicle/capsid structures accumulate at the factory periphery for capsid formation, followed by genome packaging at the vertex opposite the stargate. Internal structures mature in the cell periphery, and mature particles can be released both by cell lysis and by budding in vesicles from the host membrane.
evaluation: Claims C60-C64 describe the assembly process observed by TEM (Figure 2D and supplements). The observations are well-documented in the images, though the mechanistic details of vesicle disruption and genome packaging are partially inferred from structural observations. The budding mechanism (C64) is directly observed and compared to Marseillevirus.

result: The BsV genome was sequenced and assembled to 1,385,869 bp of linear double-stranded DNA, making it one of the largest complete viral genomes described to date and surpassing those of mimiviruses infecting Acanthamoeba spp.
evaluation: Claims C65-C68, C30-C31 report genome size from combined PacBio and Illumina sequencing. The size determination is well-supported by the sequencing methodology described in Materials and Methods, achieving 286.1x coverage with PacBio and 800x with Illumina. The comparison to other giant viruses is appropriate.

result: The BsV genome has a GC content of 25.3%, much lower than the ~50% observed for Bodo spp., suggesting the absence of large-scale horizontal gene transfer with the host in recent evolutionary history.
evaluation: Claims C69-C71 report GC content analysis shown in Figure 3. The measurement is straightforward from sequence data. The inference about horizontal gene transfer (C71) is reasonable based on the GC content disparity and is supported by citation to similar observations in other giant viruses (Raoult et al., 2004).

result: The BsV genome encodes 1227 predicted ORFs with 85% coding density, distributed roughly equally between strands. Unlike ApMV, BsV lacks a central GC skew peak indicating no organized bacterial-like origin of replication. Codon usage is highly biased toward A/T-rich codons, with predicted proteins ranging from 43 to 4840 aa (average 320 aa).
evaluation: Claims C72-C78 describe genome organization features derived from computational analysis (Figure 3). The ORF prediction using GLIMMER and subsequent analyses are standard methods. The coding density and strand distribution are directly calculable from the annotation. The comparison to ApMV (C75) is appropriate.

result: BsV has a highly conserved early promoter motif 'AAAAATTGA' identical to mimiviruses and CroV, and a poorly conserved late promoter motif 'TGCG' surrounded by AT-rich regions. ORFs are followed by palindromic sequences suggesting hairpin-based transcription termination similar to ApMV.
evaluation: Claims C79-C81 report promoter analysis using MEME and sequence analysis. The early promoter motif is well-conserved and matches known sequences in related viruses. The inference about transcription termination (C81) is reasonable based on the presence of palindromic sequences and comparison to ApMV.

result: BLASTp analysis revealed 40% of BsV ORFs are ORFans with no significant similarity to other sequences. Of annotated proteins, 27% matched eukaryotes (2% to B. saltans), 22% to NCLDVs, 9% to bacteria, and 1% to archaea. Only 45% of gene clusters are shared with related viruses like CroV and klosneuviruses.
evaluation: Claims C82-C88 report results from BLASTp analysis (Figure 4B) and gene cluster analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The methods are standard for viral genome annotation. The high proportion of ORFans (C82) is typical for giant viruses. The gene cluster analysis (C88) used OrthoMCL with appropriate parameters.

result: The BsV genome shows organized structure with essential genes for replication, translation, DNA replication and virion structure in the central region, while the periphery contains duplicated genes including 148 copies of ankyrin-repeat proteins in tandem orientation. These proteins are variable (4-17 ankyrin-repeat domains) with evidence of very recent duplication, and many contain fragments of catalytic domains from essential viral genes.
evaluation: Claims C89-C90, C127-C131 describe genome organization shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1. The central location of essential genes and peripheral duplications are clearly visible in the circular genome map. The recent duplications (C130) showing 99.7% DNA identity and the presence of gene fragments in ankyrin proteins (C131) are well-documented.

result: Functional annotation revealed 54% of BsV ORFs have unknown function, with the largest identifiable fraction involved in DNA replication and repair. BsV encodes proteins for all classes of DNA repair mechanisms, DNA replication machinery including intein-containing DNA polymerase, and 47 protein/signal modification enzymes (mostly serine/threonine kinases/phosphatases) potentially involved in host cell takeover.
evaluation: Claims C91-C96 report functional annotation results (Figure 4A). The annotation combined BLASTp and conserved domain searches, which are standard methods. The identification of specific DNA repair and replication proteins (C93-C94) is well-supported. The inference about host cell takeover (C96) is reasonable but speculative.

result: BsV encodes a rich transcription machinery including early and late transcription factors recognizing conserved motifs, RNA polymerase subunits (a,b,c,e,f,g,I), mRNA-specific RNase III, poly A polymerase, and capping enzymes. Transcription termination presumably occurs via hairpin structures similar to ApMV, and extensive cap modification suggests independence from kinetoplastid trans-splicing.
evaluation: Claims C97-C103 describe transcription machinery from functional annotation. The identification of transcription factors (C98-C99) is linked to promoter analysis (C79-C80). The inference about transcription termination (C102) is reasonable based on hairpin detection. The conclusion about independence from trans-splicing (C103) is a logical inference from the presence of complete capping machinery.

result: BsV encodes enzymes for nucleic-acid transport and metabolism including AT-specific synthesis components, and a mitochondrial carrier protein likely providing dATP/dTTP from the kinetoplast to the virus factory. Several membrane trafficking genes were identified, including a SNAP/SNARE system that appears to have been recently acquired from the host by horizontal gene transfer.
evaluation: Claims C104-C107 report functional annotation results. The identification of metabolic enzymes (C104) and membrane trafficking components (C106) is straightforward. The inference about the mitochondrial carrier function (C105) is supported by comparison to ApMV and TEM observations. The recent acquisition of SNAP/SNARE (C107) is supported by phylogenetic analysis mentioned in the text.

result: BsV encodes four major capsid proteins, one containing large insertions (4194 aa, ~7x larger than paralogs) that might create the observed halo by producing shortened fibers. The genome encodes metabolic enzymes but no complete pathways, suggesting they complement host pathways. BsV also encodes coenzyme synthetases and key steps in synthesis pathways for glutamine, histidine, isoleucine, and asparagine.
evaluation: Claims C108-C114 report structural and metabolic gene content. The capsid protein identification (C108-C109) is well-supported by annotation. The speculation about halo formation (C110) is reasonable but unproven. The observation about incomplete metabolic pathways (C112) and the inference about complementing host pathways are logical. The amino acid synthesis genes (C114) are identified by annotation.

result: BsV encodes genes putatively mediating competitive interactions with the host or other parasites, including toxins (VIP2-like protein) and antitoxins (BRO domains), partial bleomycin detox pathway, multidrug export pumps, and partial restriction modification systems.
evaluation: Claims C115-C116 report identification of defense-related genes from functional annotation. The identification of these genes is supported by sequence similarity searches. However, the actual functions in competitive interactions (C115) are inferred rather than experimentally demonstrated.

result: BsV encodes a complex but contracted translation machinery differing markedly from other Mimiviridae, showing the largest turnover resulting in net contraction. It encodes standard eukaryotic translation factors but lacks eIF-1, instead encoding host-acquired IF-2. Most strikingly, BsV lacks tRNAs but uniquely encodes tRNA repair genes (mostly recently acquired from host). BsV has few aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, with three as pseudogenes showing recent degradation, and only isoleucine-tRNA and phenylalanyl-tRNA synthetases complete.
evaluation: Claims C117-C126 describe translation machinery from annotation and comparative analysis (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplements 2-3). The absence of tRNAs (C121) is remarkable and well-documented. The presence of tRNA repair genes (C122-C123) and their phylogenetic placement are shown in supplementary figures. The pseudogenes (C125) provide evidence for recent degradation. This is a major finding distinguishing BsV from other NCLDVs.

result: The BsV genomic mobilome is dominated by inteins, autocatalytic proteinases, and self-splicing group 1 introns that spread by targeting essential genes using homing endonucleases. Inteins related to Mimiviridae/Phycodnaviridae are in DNA polymerase B, while unrelated inteins in RNA polymerase genes appear fixed (ancient invasion). Group 1 introns independently invaded RNA polymerase genes, with homing endonucleases seeding 'offspring' introns lacking endonucleases. High sequence identity (94.4%) in some offspring introns suggests recent spread. Two distinct transposon classes are also present.
evaluation: Claims C132-C141 describe mobile genetic elements shown in Figure 5 and supplements. The identification of inteins and introns is supported by sequence analysis and RT-PCR confirmation of splicing. The phylogenetic relationships (C134) and the parent-offspring intron relationships (C137-C140) are well-documented. The inference about recent vs. ancient invasions based on sequence identity is reasonable.

result: Phylogenetic analysis places BsV within the Mimiviridae, specifically clustering with large mimiviruses ('Megavirinae') and most closely with metagenomic klosneuviruses. Analysis of five concatenated NCLDV core genes reproduced this pattern, revealing three clades within Megavirinae: Acanthamoeba-infecting mimiviruses, klosneuviruses with BsV, and CroV as an outgroup. Individual gene phylogenies placed BsV within klosneuviruses in 3 of 5 cases.
evaluation: Claims C142-C147 report phylogenetic analyses (Figure 6A-B and supplements). Multiple methods were used (whole genome gene cluster analysis, concatenated core genes, individual genes) with appropriate phylogenetic approaches (RAxML, PhyML, PhyloBayes). The consistency across methods strengthens the conclusions, though some individual gene trees show variation (C147).

result: Metagenomic read recruitment from TARA Oceans DNA polymerase B sequences showed the Megavirinae are dominated by klosneuviruses, with BsV as their only isolate. This indicates BsV represents the largest group of identifiable icosahedral giant viruses in the oceans, with CroV representing the second most abundant clade. Detection in freshwater metagenomes supports global prevalence.
evaluation: Claims C148-C152 report metagenomic recruitment analysis (Figure 6C). The mapping of 256 TARA Oceans sequences to the phylogenetic tree using pplacer is an appropriate method. The conclusion that BsV represents the most abundant group (C149, C151) is well-supported by the read distribution. However, the analysis is limited to DNA polymerase B sequences, which may not fully represent all giant viruses.

result: The SNAP/SNARE membrane fusion system in BsV appears recently acquired from the host and could mediate pH-dependent membrane fusion. The authors propose a phagocytosis-based infection strategy where BsV is ingested through the cytostome, phagocytosed, and transported to the cell posterior where viral SNAP/SNARE interacts with host counterparts to fuse membranes upon acidification, releasing the genome. SNAP/SNARE proteins must be present in mature virions and might also recruit membrane vesicles during particle maturation.
evaluation: Claims C153-C158 propose an infection mechanism based on the presence of SNAP/SNARE genes and TEM observations. While the phylogenetic evidence for recent acquisition (C153) is mentioned, the proposed infection mechanism (C155-C156) is speculative and not directly tested. The requirement for SNAP/SNARE in virions (C157) and the role in vesicle recruitment (C158) are hypotheses requiring experimental validation.

result: The authors propose that BsV's homing endonuclease-containing introns and inteins function as competitive weapons against related viruses. During superinfection, these elements would cleave the competitor's genome at unoccupied loci while the intron/intein-containing virus remains protected, reducing the competitor's replication. Similar mechanisms exist in phages. Supporting evidence includes fragmented RNA polymerase genes with apparent homing endonucleases in related klosneuviruses, and non-fixed inteins in other giant viruses suggesting past invasions and ongoing selection.
evaluation: Claims C159-C168 propose a novel competitive mechanism. While the presence of homing endonucleases is well-documented (C160, C164 supported by citations to phage systems), the proposed competitive function (C161-C163) is speculative and untested in BsV. The supporting evidence from related viruses (C165-C166) is suggestive but circumstantial. The hypothesis is creative and testable but requires experimental validation, particularly demonstration of superinfection and genome cleavage.

result: The absence of tRNAs in BsV might be an adaptation to unusual kinetoplastid RNA modification including tRNA editing. BsV likely cannot replicate this editing and thus relies on host tRNAs, encoding tRNA repair genes to maintain the tRNA pool. Most virus-encoded aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases might not recognize highly modified host tRNAs and are degrading, with three recognizable pseudogenes arguing for evolutionarily recent degradation.
evaluation: Claims C169-C173 propose an explanation for the absence of tRNAs. The observation of tRNA absence (C121) and presence of repair genes (C122-C123) is well-supported. However, the proposed mechanism (C169-C172) is speculative. The inference about recent degradation from pseudogenes (C173) is reasonable but the functional explanation requires experimental validation, such as demonstrating that BsV actually uses host tRNAs and that the repair genes are functional.

result: The turnover in translational machinery components in BsV and klosneuviruses, combined with diverse gene origins, suggests the translation machinery in giant viruses results from rapid adaptation via horizontal gene transfer rather than being ancient. BsV demonstrates these genes can be readily purged if not required in a new host, providing evidence that NCLDV translation machinery is a homoplasic trait not derived from a common ancestor.
evaluation: Claims C174-C176, C190 present an important evolutionary conclusion supported by the comparative analysis (Figure 4C) and phylogenetic evidence. The observation of gene loss and turnover in BsV is well-documented. The conclusion about homoplasy is supported by the data and consistent with recent proposals (Schulz et al., 2017). However, more extensive phylogenetic analysis of individual translation genes would strengthen this conclusion.

result: The 148 ankyrin-repeat protein copies in BsV's genomic periphery represent an expanded genomic accordion, with nearly identical sequences at genome ends consistent with recent duplications. The authors propose these proteins function as decoy defense mechanisms, with fusion proteins containing fragments of essential viral genes mimicking targets of host antiviral defenses. By binding host factors via ankyrin-repeat domains (similar to vaccinia virus), they might immobilize and potentially degrade them via ubiquitin-dependent pathways, possibly explaining persistent cell survival during infection.
evaluation: Claims C177-C185 describe ankyrin-repeat expansion and propose a decoy defense function. The genomic accordion observation (C177-C178) is well-supported by sequence data (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The known functions in poxviruses and bacteria (C179-C180) are properly cited. However, the proposed decoy mechanism (C181-C183) is speculative and not experimentally tested in BsV. The connection to persistent cells (C184) is particularly speculative. The hypothesis is creative but requires functional validation.

result: BsV exemplifies genomic plasticity in giant viruses through the genomic accordion mechanism allowing large-scale expansions/contractions via non-homologous recombination. Recent duplications demonstrate genome expansion in action, exemplifying mechanisms leading to genome gigantism. The function of expanding genes suggests strong evolutionary pressure from virus-host arms races driving genomic expansion. Plasticity is also evident in translational machinery showing recent gene loss and rapid adaptation. Invasion of selfish elements in essential genes suggests interference competition among related viruses.
evaluation: Claims C186-C189, C191 present overarching conclusions about genomic plasticity. These are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence: the ankyrin-repeat duplications (C127-C131), translation machinery turnover (C117-C126), and mobile element invasions (C132-C141). The genomic accordion concept is supported by the data and properly cited (Elde et al., 2012). The inference about arms race pressure (C188) is reasonable given the nature of the expanding genes.

result: BsV is the first described DNA virus infecting kinetoplastids or any member of the supergroup Excavata, and is the first isolate of the klosneuviruses, a subfamily within Mimiviridae previously known only from metagenomic data.
evaluation: Claims C18-C20, C33-C34 state the novelty of BsV. These claims are supported by the phylogenetic placement (C142-C147) showing BsV clusters with metagenomic klosneuviruses, and by the host identification as B. saltans (Excavata). The claim about being the first DNA virus of kinetoplastids appears accurate based on the literature context provided.

result: The introduction provides background on viruses in aquatic ecosystems, giant virus discovery history, and kinetoplastid biology. Key points include: viruses are abundant in aquatic systems killing ~20% of biomass daily with major biogeochemical impacts; giant viruses exist alongside smaller viruses; the first giant virus (later in Mimiviridae) infected a flagellate initially identified as Bodo sp. (later Cafeteria roenbergensis); mimivirus discovery transformed understanding of giant viruses; most isolated giant viruses infect Acanthamoeba spp.; kinetoplastids have unusual RNA editing, a kinetoplast containing up to 25% of cellular DNA, and include human/livestock pathogens.
evaluation: Claims C1-C29 provide literature context and established knowledge. All claims are supported by appropriate citations (Suttle 2007, Garza and Suttle 1995, Fischer et al. 2010, La Scola et al. 2003, Raoult et al. 2004, etc.). These are background claims establishing the scientific context rather than novel findings from this study.

result: The BsV genome exhibits evidence of significant genome rearrangements and recent adaptations to its host.
evaluation: Claims C35-C36 are general statements supported by multiple specific findings: genome rearrangements evidenced by disrupted ORFs and duplications (C127-C131), and recent adaptations shown by recently acquired genes (C107, C120, C123), pseudogenes (C125), and recent intron/intein invasions (C140). These summary claims are well-supported by the detailed analyses.
